verdict: The science is now exact and the page is honest. I re-derived every number in the prose from colour-science's CIE tables with an independent script, and every one reproduces: 0.0 / 19.4 / 30.0 / 18.8 / 24.6 / 3.5. The pair matches for the 1931, 1964 and 2015 2-degree observers (0.0 / 0.0 / 0.007), and the large-field 2015 observer gives 0.11. The cone signals are 0.312 / 0.306 / 0.300, and the 17x, 8% / 44%, 4-band / 12-band, 7-crossings and 46 / 35 / 19 numbers all check, as does every exercise answer (47.1; 4.0 to 4.7, 3.2 and 0.4; 0.9 / 3.1 / 5.7 / 4.5; 30% / 32% and up to 28; 83 of 100). validate and browser-check pass clean, 21 of 21 self-tests pass, the clean-room rule holds and project.json mirrors the page exactly. What stands between this lesson and socks-off is its 'why'. The tagline promises 'Here is why', but the worked examples point at the wrong part of the spectrum. Step 2 uses 680 nm and step 3 quotes 700 nm and 400 nm, where the eye is nearly blind. A 25-point bump at 680 nm moves the color by only 1.1 even under the warm bulb, and giving Fog Pebble's red end leaves the split at 21.4. The pair really splits because of the shop light's dark green gap. Pebble sends back 49% at 520 nm and Fog 11%, and only 3% of the shop light's light falls between 500 and 535 nm, against 10% for the warm bulb and 15% for daylight. So the page's own picture contradicts its example: Fog, the paint with less deep red, is the one that turns dusty rose under the warm bulb. Retelling steps 2 and 3 around that green gap (copy I give below, every number checked) would turn the explainer into a real aha. Also fix one falsifiable sentence in step 4 ('no single handle can move unseen'). Rework the one exercise that only re-asks a sentence from step 5, and define a few leftover terms. All of this is copy work.

findings.area: teaching / correctness of the 'why' (steps 2 and 3, figure 3)
findings.title: The worked examples explain the split with the far red and violet ends, but this pair splits in the shop light's dark green gap; the hero's own colors contradict the example
findings.evidence: index.html:371 (step 2): 'Take one wavelength, 680 nm, a deep red. Pebble sends back 52% of it and Fog only 20% ... the warm bulb gives out about 17 times as much of that light ..., so the same gap ... counts about 17 times as much under the warm bulb.' index.html:394 (step 3): 'At 700 nm Pebble sends back 62% ... and Fog 11%; at 400 nm ... 14% and 45%.' The numbers are right (oracle2.json: 51.8/19.7%, ratio 17.24; 62.4/10.8%, 14.4/44.8%), but these wavelengths barely matter. A 25-point bump at 680 nm changes the color by 0.08 under the shop light, 1.14 under the warm bulb and 0.51 in daylight. At 700 nm the changes are 0.03, 0.31 and 0.12 (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user/f017b37b-956c-5936-ade0-801c06b2aa0a/scratchpad/cameo/c2/qa2-content/bump680.py). Giving Fog Pebble's values from 640 to 780 nm leaves the split at 21.4 under the warm bulb and 31.1 in daylight (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user/f017b37b-956c-5936-ade0-801c06b2aa0a/scratchpad/cameo/c2/qa2-content/where2.py): the red end does not cause the split. Where the split really comes from (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user/f017b37b-956c-5936-ade0-801c06b2aa0a/scratchpad/cameo/c2/qa2-content/where.py): under the warm bulb, 480 to 540 nm supplies 0.035 of the 0.048 L-cone difference and 0.063 of the 0.068 M-cone difference. Pebble sends back 49% at 520 nm and Fog 11%. The FL11 table falls to 0.83 to 2.33 between 505 and 530 nm, against 72.8 at 545 nm. Only 3.0% of the shop light's 400 to 700 nm light lies in 500 to 535 nm, against 9.5% for the warm bulb and 14.7% for daylight. A 25-point bump at 515 nm changes the color by 1.4 under the shop light, 6.8 under the warm bulb and 7.5 in daylight. The page then contradicts the inference its example invites. Pebble 'sends back much more deep red', yet under the warm bulb the hero shows 'Pebble #A89273, tan · Fog #AB7D7B, dusty rose' (a* -2.5 against +10.1; walk1.json lamp_A; shots/hero-A.png). The less-red paint is the pinker one, and nothing on the page explains why. Figure 3 suffers for the same reason (shots/fig3-pebble-shop.png against shots/fig3-fog-shop.png). Under the shop light the two paints' light differs by only 21% (L1 over 400 to 700 nm; it was 54% for the round-1 pair; /tmp/claude-0/-home-user/f017b37b-956c-5936-ade0-801c06b2aa0a/scratchpad/cameo/c2/qa2-content/lightdiff.py). Their big difference sits in the lamp's dark gap, so 'the curves change, the bars do not' barely shows.
findings.fix: Replace the step-2 example with: 'Take one wavelength, 520 nm, a green. Pebble sends back 49% of it and Fog only 11%. The shop light has a dark gap there, between its blue-green glow and its green line: only 3% of its light falls between 500 and 535 nm, against 10% for the warm bulb and 15% for daylight. So the same gap between Pebble and Fog counts far less under the shop light. Raise a curve by 25 points around 515 nm and the color changes by 1.4 under the shop light, 6.8 under the warm bulb and 7.5 in daylight.' Step 3 numbers: 'At 520 nm Pebble sends back 49% of the light and Fog 11%; at 475 nm it is the other way round, 22% and 38%. Yet under the shop light both give 0.312, 0.306 and 0.300.' Then add a sentence to 'The shop light makes this easy': '...and where they differ most, between 500 and 535 nm, the shop light is nearly dark. That is why Pebble, with its extra green, turns tan and then sage once the warm bulb or daylight fills the gap, while Fog, short of green, turns dusty rose and then mauve.' In figure 3, draw the other paint's light as a dashed outline and shade 500 to 535 nm with the label 'Pebble's extra green falls in this gap'. Optionally add the same subtle shading on the hero's paper strips under the shop light. If you want to keep a red example, use it for the opposite lesson: 'beyond 680 nm your eye is nearly blind, so even big differences there barely count under any lamp'. Re-run the oracle on whichever sentences you keep.

findings.title: 'Under the shop light no single handle can move unseen' is false for four of the 13 handles, and a visitor can disprove it on the page
findings.evidence: index.html:418: 'Under the shop light no single handle can move unseen: lift any one of them and the numbers change.' I lifted each of Pebble's handles by 25 points and measured the change under the shop light (oracle2.json single_handle_lift_25pts_FL11): 400 nm 0.68, 650 nm 0.16, 675 nm 0.10 and 700 nm 0.03. All four are below the page's own 'about 1 is just noticeable', where its verdict reads 'Identical to the eye'. The other nine range from 2.8 to 25.6 (550 nm). In Make my own pair with the lock off, I dragged the 700 nm end from 62% to about 90% under the shop light. The status read 'Shop light 0.0 · warm bulb 0.1' (walk3.json free700). Exercise 3 then teaches the opposite: a 25-point red bump at 650 nm shows only 0.9 under the shop light.
findings.fix: Rewrite: 'Under the shop light most single handles cannot move unseen: lift the 550 nm handle alone by 25 points and the difference jumps to about 26. Only the handles at the two ends get away with it: your eye is nearly blind at 400 nm and beyond 650 nm, and the shop light gives out little deep red (exercise 3 shows this). But the handles can also move together, some up and some down...' The rest of the paragraph can stay.

findings.title: Exercise 1 re-asks a sentence from step 5 instead of applying it to a new case, and the exercises' promise overstates
findings.evidence: index.html:450 (step 5): 'in that model two paints that send back the same share at 589 nm match exactly, however different they look by day.' Exercise 1 (index.html:480) asks whether two paints that both send back 40% at 589 nm match under the street lamp. The answer is that sentence, and figures 4 and 5 already show it. The section intro (index.html:476) promises 'Each question applies the idea to something the demos above did not show.' Exercise 5 is also shown directly by figure 6: the answer itself says to choose Shop light there and switch paints. Exercises 2, 3 and 4 are real transfers.
findings.fix: Make exercise 1 a reasoning step. For example: 'Under the street lamp, paint P sends back 60% at 589 nm and paint Q 20%; by day P is deep blue and Q bright yellow. Under the street lamp, which looks lighter, and which looks more colorful?' Choices: 'P lighter, neither colorful' / 'Q lighter' / 'They match'. Answer: only the 589 nm share is left, so P looks lighter and both are shades of one orange. Design P and Q by script, print the numbers and add a self-test case. Or keep exercise 1 and change the intro to 'Each question applies the idea to a new case.'

findings.title: A few terms still appear before, or without, a plain definition
findings.evidence: First screen, chips caption (index.html:276): 'one for each kind of cone'. Cones are defined only in step 3. The hero lamp caption (index.html:245) reads 'CIE table FL11'; CIE is spelled out only in step 1. More, Numbers table (index.html:325-328): the 'L*', 'a*', 'b*' columns and the note 'L*, a* and b* are CIELAB against that white' are never explained. 'White point' appears in the self-check line (index.html:564), the About (index.html:577) and every self-test name ('White point of CIE standard illuminant A is ...'), and is never defined. The About lists 'sRGB' without explanation. These are small, but unexplained terms were the owner's complaint about day 1.
findings.fix: Chips caption: 'one for each kind of cone (the three kinds of light-sensing cell in your eye)'. Make CIE in the hero caption an <abbr title="International Commission on Illumination, which publishes standard tables of light and color vision">. Numbers note: 'L* is lightness (0 black to 100 white), a* runs from green (-) to red (+) and b* from blue (-) to yellow (+): CIELAB, the CIE's color space in which CIEDE2000 measures differences.' Self-check line: 'the color of each CIE lamp's light (its white point)'. About: 'sRGB, the standard color space of screens'.

findings.title: Small wording slips: self-contradiction, awkward cross-references, mild overstatements and naming drift
findings.evidence: (a) index.html:419: 'only the two lamps this page models can still tell your paint from Pebble: the sodium street lamp, by at most about 3.4, and the smooth glow, by almost nothing.' Telling two paints apart 'by almost nothing' is a contradiction; my walk along the one free direction gives 0.006 for the glow and 3.38 for sodium (oracle2.json four_lock_max_split). (b) index.html:395 'What this page simplifies says which.' and index.html:472 'as What this page simplifies explains': a heading used as a sentence subject, unmarked. (c) index.html:449 'The lab tests this fairly.' is vague. (d) Figure 5 labels the shop light '4000 K' and the smooth glow '3999 K', yet the text calls them the same color. The careful reader asks why (the CIE nominal is 4000 K, and the computed CCT is 3998.6 K). (e) index.html:551 'When a photo looks right, the mix is a metamer of the real thing.' Looking right is not the same three numbers. (f) index.html:499 'the smallest difference was 3.2'. That is true of the page's 2,000 Gaussian lamps, but a single line at 655 nm gives 2.8 (oracle2.json ex2_min_over_line_lamps), so 3.2 reads as a floor it is not. (g) The sodium lamp has four names: 'Sodium lamp (modeled)' (figure 4), 'Sodium street lamp' (figure 5, More), 'street lamp' (exercise 1) and 'sodium lamp' (editor status). (h) The hint is stale: after a find it keeps saying 'Now press Wiggle, or make your own pair.' while Fog is wiggling and after the visitor has done both (walk1.json wiggle_mid and wiggle_end).
findings.fix: (a) 'Then only the sodium street lamp can still tell your paint from Pebble, by at most about 3.4; even the smooth glow sees less than 0.01.' (b) Make both cross-references links: '(see What this page simplifies)'. (c) 'The lab makes it a fair test:'. (d) Label the shop light 'about 4000 K', or add 'its color matches a 3999 K glow' to the figure note. (e) 'When a photo looks right, the mix is close to a metamer of the real thing.' (f) Add '(a single line at 655 nm gets it down to 2.8: still far from a match)'. (g) Use 'sodium street lamp' everywhere text allows, and 'sodium lamp' only in tight chips. (h) After the visitor has wiggled, drop 'Now press Wiggle'. After the editor has been used, drop 'or make your own pair'.

findings.title: On desktop the editor drops the key for its dotted lines, so three vertical lines go unexplained
findings.evidence: hero.js:510 writes the long legend ('... · dotted lines: where the held lamp shines brightest') only when the canvas is at least 560 px wide. The editor canvas is 520 px wide at 1280x800 (walk3.json canvas.w = 520), so desktop visitors see only 'dashed: Pebble · solid: your paint' above three dotted lines at the shop light's lines (shots/editor-after3.png).
findings.fix: Lower the threshold to about 480 px, or move the legend into an HTML line under the chart: 'dashed: Pebble · solid: your paint · dotted: where the held lamp shines brightest'.

findings.title: One concept is never taught under its name, one source title is a fragment, and one citation's support is unverified
findings.evidence: project.json concepts includes 'chromatic adaptation', but the page never uses the term; it says 'Your eye adjusts to the color of a lamp'. The source title 'term 17-23-008, metameric colour stimuli' (project.json and the About) is a fragment that means nothing on its own. The x046 OP27 paper is cited for 'the CIE illuminants LED-B1 to LED-B5 represent the widespread blue-chip phosphor LEDs', but REVISE-1-report.md says the reviser opened no URL and saw it only in a search result. My search found the paper listed for the 2019 CIE session under the title 'A colour graphic for real complex scenes, applied to LED illuminants'. It confirmed neither the OP27 number nor that the paper makes this claim. The claim itself is true, and the CIE LED data-table page and the U.S. Department of Energy pages, both already cited, carry it.
findings.fix: Replace the 'chromatic adaptation' concept with 'observer metamerism' or 'illuminant', or name the term once in 'What you see' ('this adjustment is called chromatic adaptation'). Retitle the vocabulary source 'CIE International Lighting Vocabulary, term 17-23-008, metameric colour stimuli'. Drop the x046 entry, or open it and quote where it says this, and let the CIE LED data table and the DOE pages carry the LED sentence.

findings.title: The explainer never states the idea in one closing line
findings.evidence: The explainer opens with the misconception ('a paint simply has a color ... and light only shows it', index.html:339). It then runs straight from the screen reveal into the exercises, 'Where you meet it' and the limits. No sentence resolves the misconception in plain words. The idea is spread across steps 2 to 4, and the page is long: about 4,100 visible words with the answers open (walk2.json pageText).
findings.fix: At the end of 'Your screen is a metamer machine', before the exercises, add one bold takeaway: 'So a color is not in the paint. It is the lamp's light times the paint's curve, squeezed by your eye into three numbers. Two paints match when those three numbers agree, and a different lamp can pull them apart.'

praise: Every number in the prose reproduces independently from colour-science's CIE tables (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user/f017b37b-956c-5936-ade0-801c06b2aa0a/scratchpad/cameo/c2/qa2-content/oracle2.py, oracle2.json). The pair numbers are 0.0 / 19.4 / 30.0 / 18.8 / 24.6 / 3.5, with lightness 5.0 and 6.5 L* under the warm bulb and in daylight. The observer match is 0.0 for 1964, 0.007 for 2015 2-degree and 0.11 for 2015 10-degree. Also exact: the cone signals 0.312 / 0.306 / 0.300; 52/20% at 680 nm, 62/11% at 700 nm and 14/45% at 400 nm; the 17.2x ratio; 4 bands against 12; 7 crossings with one at 543 nm; gaps of at most 5.7 points at the lines; 8% against 44%; 46/35/19; x,y (0.3805, 0.3769) and (0.3805, 0.3768); every exercise answer; and the four-lock bound of 3.4.

The observer-robust redesign is real and honestly told. The pair matches for three CIE observers, and 'What this page simplifies' says plainly that the wiggle holds only for the 1931 one. I checked that too: most wiggle frames break the 1964 match, at times above 10 (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user/f017b37b-956c-5936-ade0-801c06b2aa0a/scratchpad/cameo/c2/qa2-content/wigglestats.mjs).

The hero wiggle is the screenshot. Fog's curve thrashes over its frozen block under a 'Color unchanged' badge, while the was/now swatches flicker apart under the warm bulb. The readout says it in plain words: 'Fog under the shop light: unchanged (0.0)' / 'Under the warm bulb: 34.3 from the original' (shots/hero-wiggle-mid.png).

Exercise 4 (a lamp with two lines, then the three-line and four-line twist) is a superb transfer of the null-space idea, and the page proves it live: 200 wiggles keep the heights at 450 and 600 nm while the curve moves up to 17 points, and with four lines the heights move. Exercises 2 and 3 are also genuine new cases.
Every exercise prints 'Computed by this page just now', and 21 of 21 self-tests are offered to the visitor in plain language.

Clean room and honesty: no vendor names, logos or UI. Sources are the CIE, ASTM, the U.S. Department of Energy, universities, a science museum and encyclopedias. Every modeled lamp is labeled, and the limits are candid ('Bigger than life', observer metamerism, the 40% tint).
Definitions now arrive where they are needed: nm, wavelength, illuminant, kelvin and color temperature, Planck's law, phosphor, the x and y of a light, observer, metamer and observer metamerism.

project.json mirrors the page exactly: <title>, h1 and title; tagline; intro (51 words, a 25-word first sentence); description equal to the meta description; makingOf equal to the About text; 28 identical sources. validate and browser-check report 0 errors and 0 warnings.
